prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational
Asset type: Dino Atlas period-subdivided ecosystem gallery image for children ages 5-14
Primary request: Create a completely new, realistic but non-graphic 4:5 portrait paleoart scene of exactly two dinosaurs coexisting in the Late Triassic Cancha de Bochas Member of the Ischigualasto Formation seasonal floodplain. This visualizes same-stratigraphic-member coexistence only; it must not imply an observed interaction.
Input images: Image 1 is anatomy-only reference for Eoraptor lunensis. Image 2 is anatomy-only reference for Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis. Do not copy either reference's composition, pose, color scheme, lighting, or background.
Scene/backdrop: Dry seasonal Ischigualasto floodplain viewed from a high diagonal, near-top-down angle. Make the land itself visually distinctive: concentric ring-like paleosol patterns surrounding a shallow circular depression, sparse low vegetation, patches of cracked sediment, muted oxidized ochre, dusty sage and mineral gray. No modern grass, flowers, or dense forest.
Subject placement and spatial signature: Exactly two animals total. Put one Eoraptor in the upper third of the portrait frame and one visibly larger Herrerasaurus in the lower third. Separate them with a broad, clearly empty band of patterned ground. Their body axes and travel directions must be different: Eoraptor walks toward the upper-left, Herrerasaurus pauses or walks toward the lower-right. They do not look at each other. No converging movement, pursuit, attack, eye-line crossing, contact, blood, carcass, prey, eggs, nests, or other animals.
Eoraptor anatomy: 1.2-1.3 meter small early saurischian, low triangular head, moderate low S-shaped neck (not long or swan-like), lightly built torso, exactly two short robust forelimbs visibly separate from the body, exactly two hindlimbs, each hind foot readable with three main forward toes plus a small first toe when perspective allows, and one long continuous balancing tail. No beak, no raptor sickle claw, no dromaeosaur look, no feathers, no extra limbs, no fused limbs.
Herrerasaurus anatomy: visibly much larger than Eoraptor, long low predatory head, moderately deep trunk, exactly two non-tiny forelimbs visibly separate from the torso, compact hands with three main fingers readable, exactly two strong hindlimbs, two complete feet, and one long continuous balancing tail. No Tyrannosaurus-style tiny arms, no giant head, no extra limbs, no fused limbs.
Composition/framing: Portrait 4:5. High oblique/near-top-down scientific field-observation camera. Both animals must be completely inside the frame with generous padding. Every silhouette must be isolated against open ground. All four limbs per animal category as applicable—both forelimbs, both hindlimbs, every foot, both hands, and each full tail tip—must be visible and unoccluded. No cropping, foreground occlusion, dust cloud, motion blur, extreme foreshortening, overlapping bodies, or vegetation covering anatomy.
Style/medium: Highly polished natural-history museum paleoart, anatomically legible, realistic skin texture, restrained natural colors, age-appropriate for 5-14, no gore.
Lighting/mood: Clear warm late-afternoon light with short soft shadows that help separate each limb from the ground; calm observational mood.
Text: none.
Constraints: Exactly two animals and no more. Preserve species size contrast. All anatomy and silhouettes fully visible. The circular paleosol geometry is environmental, not a decorative frame around the animals.
Avoid: text, labels, watermark, border, infographic arrows, fantasy anatomy, extra toes dominating, duplicated limbs, missing limbs, merged feet, broken tails, chase narrative, combat, threat display, direct interaction, dramatic cinematic confrontation.

anatomy.verdict: Exactly two animals; Eoraptor is visibly smaller and preserves a low triangular head, short paired forelimbs, paired hindlimbs, readable feet, and a complete tail; Herrerasaurus is larger and preserves a long low head, paired non-tiny forelimbs with compact hands, paired strong hindlimbs, complete feet, and a complete tail. risks: The high camera and intentional size contrast make Eoraptor's individual fingers and small first toes less legible than in a dedicated single-animal anatomy plate.
Herrerasaurus hand digits and far-side foot details are readable at original size but remain small; do not use this scene as a hand or pedal anatomy reference.
